\begin{abstract}
Differential privacy in federated learning is evaluated along two axes,
privacy and utility. On battery-powered edge devices a third decides whether a
configuration is deployable at all, and it is not reported. We measure the
energy cost of client-level differential privacy with NVML hardware counters
differenced around each federated round, sweeping the privacy budget on
UCI-HAR, whose clients are the individual study participants, and on
CIFAR-10. The per-round cost is power times time, and only one factor
transfers: private rounds draw $1.19\times$ the power of non-private ones on
both datasets to within $0.5\%$, while the duration factor differs
($1.27\times$ and $1.13\times$). Neither varies systematically with the
budget, so everything budget-dependent acts through the number of rounds --
the larger term. Measured as energy-to-target-accuracy, privacy is free at
$0.40$ accuracy on UCI-HAR, costs $5.7\times$ at $0.70$ where only
$\varepsilon \ge 4$ arrives, and cannot buy $0.85$ at any expenditure. Because
the cost is paid in joules it inherits the local carbon intensity: an
$18.8\times$ range between Algeria's grid and Norway's for an identical
guarantee, on both datasets. We also report two hazards specific to measuring
a privacy mechanism. Deriving noise multipliers inside the timed loop
reproduces an entire apparent $\varepsilon$ trend; and calibrating the noise
against \emph{expected} client participation under-charges the clients
sampled most, so all 29 of our private runs spend more than their stated
budget, by up to $22\%$.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
federated learning, differential privacy, energy efficiency, green AI, carbon
footprint, edge computing, human activity recognition
\end{IEEEkeywords}
